podcast.title: New Wave Breakthrough (Summer 1979)
podcast.body: The Knack was among the power pop bands that achieved their biggest hits during the summer of 1979, which was recognized as the breakthrough summer for New Wave in America. "as power pop bands like Cheap Trick. The neck, and the cars. All scored their biggest hits to date."

podcast.title: Nuke the Knack T-shirts (1979)
podcast.body: In 1979, discerning rock fans expressed their disdain for The Knack by wearing "Nuke the NAC t-shirts" due to the band's faux Beatles imagery, sexist lyrics, and the song's chart success in a disco-heavy year. "Descerning Rock fans even wore Nuke the NAC t-shirts that year."

podcast.body: The Knack contributed to the soundtrack for *Reality Bites*, a key film in the "slacker culture" movement released in 1994. The soundtrack also featured other notable artists like U2 and Lisa Loeb. "The NAC, you two, and the Massive Hit for Lisa Loeb stay, I missed you."

podcast.title: "Good Girls Don't" 45 Sleeve Model
podcast.body: The person named Sharona, who inspired the hit song "My Sharona," also appeared on the cover of the 45 sleeve for the song "Good Girls Don't." On the cover, she was depicted wearing a white tank top and Levi's. "And yes, that is Sharona in the white tank top and Levi's on the cover of the 45 sleeve for Good Girls Don't."

podcast.title: Backlash from Rapid Success
podcast.body: Despite their phenomenal commercial success, The Knack experienced severe backlash due to how quickly they became popular. However, their success demonstrated to other record labels that signing New Wave bands could be a profitable strategy during an economic downturn. "And even though the NAC experienced some severe backlash because they became so successful so fast, other record labels realized that their way out of the economic doldrums might just be to sign more new wave bands."

podcast.title: Early Failures and Breakthrough
podcast.body: The Knack, originating in Detroit with singer Doug Feiger, initially faced total failure, with all their demos being rejected by record companies. Their breakthrough came when guitarist Bertene Vaire presented a guitar riff and drum part, which combined with Feiger's lyrics inspired by Sharona Elperin, led to their hit song "My Sharona." "At first, Doug and his band were total failures. All their demos had been rejected by all the record companies they approached."

podcast.title: Post-"My Sharona" Career Trajectory
podcast.body: Following the immense success of "My Sharona," The Knack did not achieve another hit of comparable magnitude. Despite continuing to make music after their chart-topping single, they were never able to replicate the widespread commercial success of "My Sharona." "They still made music, but they would never ever have a hit like my Sharona again."

podcast.title: Sharona Elperin as Inspiration
podcast.body: The song "My Sharona" was written by Doug Feiger in about 15 minutes, inspired by his infatuation with 17-year-old Sharona Elperin, whom he had recently met. Sharona Elperin is currently a real estate agent in California. "It was shortly after that, though, that Doug ran into a 17-year-old girl named Sharona Elperin."

xref.title: Contemporary Powerpop Sound
xref.body: Recorded in 1972, their song "Roadrunner" is noted for sounding "every bit as modern powerpop as anything by the strokes or slone, the new pranographers, the Danny Warhol's, Jimmy Eat World, and even the Go-Ghosts, and the knack and blondie and the Romantics," demonstrating its ahead-of-its-time quality. "It was recorded in 1972, and it is every bit as modern powerpop as anything by the strokes or slone, the new pranographers, the Danny Warhol's, Jimmy Eat World, and even the Go-Ghosts, and the knack and blondie and the Romantics."

xref.title: Extensive Influences
xref.body: Weezer's influences are broad and deep within the Powerpop lineage, including foundational bands like The Beatles, The Ramones, Cheap Trick, The Knack, and The Cars, as well as The Pixies. This wide array of influences supports the argument that they are currently the leading Powerpop band in the world. "Their influences include the Beatles, the Ramones, Cheap Trick, the Nack, the Cars, the Pixies, ensure just about every single band that we've mentioned so far."

xref.title: Initial Dislike of the Precision Bass
xref.body: Bill Black, the bass player for Elvis Presley, initially harbored a strong dislike for the Fender Precision Bass. He reportedly struggled to master the instrument and found it difficult to play. "Then came Bill Black, the bass player for Elvis Presley, although it is said that he initially really, really hated the thing because he just couldn't quite get the knack of playing."

xref.title: Precursors to Other Powerpop Bands
xref.body: Big Star predated other successful Powerpop bands of the 1970s, such as Badfinger, Todd Rundgren, The Raspberries, Cheap Trick, and The Knack, establishing the genre's foundation before its wider recognition. "There were other Powerpop bands in the 70s who had hits. There was Bad Finger and Todd Rungren. We had the raspberries, Cheap Trick, the Nack, but Big Star was there before all of them."
